Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00649

Another objection to those who say that a possible event has an actual possibility in the world is this: possibility requires a relation to the thing that is possible. If possibility is only an idea in the mind, then it relates to something the mind has imagined. But if it is an actual feature in the world, it must relate to something that exists in the world. A real relation to something that does not exist in the world is not possible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00650

The mind can picture something that might exist and judge that it could either exist or not exist. It can judge this simply by considering what the thing is. That is possibility in itself. Or it may make the judgment by considering the thing’s causes, the readiness of what can receive it, the absence of things that oppose it, and the removal of what would prevent it from coming about. This is readiness for a thing to exist—a kind of possibility through preparation.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00651
4. Features of what is possible in itself
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00652

We have delayed discussing the features of what is necessary in itself until the section on divine matters. They belong to a different kind of inquiry, and their subject is too exalted to place among the general rules about concepts and ideas drawn from things. We have mentioned only a few points needed to make the path of reasoning clear; we will return to them later by a sacred and higher path.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00653

A gathering place: Just as what has always been necessary is simple, one, and indivisible, what is possible in itself involves being made of parts, mixing, joining, and pairing. Every possible thing is a composite. A possible essence cannot stand on its own without existence; and a possible existence has no definite character without some degree of limitation and weakness, from which the essence arises and from which the ideas that describe possibility are drawn. Its particular effects follow from that limited level. The broad, general effects that flow from the Necessary Being reach every recipient. The particular effects found in each possible existence also come from the First Source, though speaking of them as its effects is a comparison, as we will explain.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00654

Every possible thing can therefore be understood through two aspects: what it is and the fact that it exists. Each involves the other, even when we consider the narrowest kinds and the broadest classes. Considered only in terms of what it is, a possible thing has the capacity to exist but does not exist by itself. Through its cause, it actually exists. Apart from existence, its nature is sheer “not-being”; existence comes to it through its cause. From these two sides, every possible thing has both potentiality and actuality. Nothing apart from the Necessary Being is entirely free of potentiality. Everything else combines these two meanings. Potentiality and possibility are like matter; actuality and necessity are like form. Every possible thing therefore has a composite structure, with one aspect like matter and another like form. True simplicity cannot exist in the world of possibility—not in the basic kinds of substance, nor in their properties and qualities.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00655

Oneness, too, belongs in its fullest sense only to the divine reality. The idea of any possible kind of thing can apply to more than one individual. Even a particular thing belongs to a broader description, whether that description comes from what it is or from a feature it happens to have. Other things could share that description. Something else may prevent those other individuals from existing, but nothing in the description itself rules them out. No possible thing, then, is absolutely one and unique. It is called one only in relation to something more divided and shared. The oneness of possible things is weak in its simplicity: their “oneness” is a union that includes some multiplicity. The single aspect in them is a shadow of God’s pure oneness, which gives all other kinds of unity, each at a lower level than the one before.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00656

The closest is the individual oneness of the First Intellect, which is the same as its existence and the way it is made distinct. Next comes the oneness of the other active intellects, then the oneness of souls, then of forms. Below these is the connected oneness of a body, which contains multiplicity only as a potential. Then comes the oneness of prime matter, which gathers multiplicity and unfolds it into the realities of kinds and individuals. This is a vague, general oneness, like a broad class.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00657

There is another side to this. Just as possibility is involved in being made of parts, anything made of parts is possible in itself. Consider a whole simply as a whole, without looking at any particular part. It cannot be independent in its existence or in its nonexistence. That very dependence shows that it is possible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00658

As for imagined combinations of two necessary things, two impossible things, a necessary thing with an impossible one, or two opposites or contradictories taken together, these are only ideas. They do not name realities that stand on their own as substances. Such ideas cannot be true of themselves in the usual sense; they fall under their opposites. The idea of a partner to God, for example, is not itself a partner to God. Rather, it is a mental quality produced by the imagination and by confused thinking. The same applies to these imagined combinations. Their necessity or impossibility depends on whether their parts are necessary or impossible. They have only the status of dependence, need, possibility, and relation, whether considered in terms of existence or nonexistence. What is impossible in the case of contradictories or opposites is their being together in one thing—not the realities of the contradictories or opposites themselves, whatever their other status.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00659

There is another subtle point. Unity applies to the divisions of any meaning that can be the subject of a general rule. When we say that every thing made of parts is possible, we mean a whole that really forms one thing. When we say that everything necessary in itself is simple, we mean that such a being is one undivided reality. And when we make a rule about animals, we mean things that each have one animal nature.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00660

A supposed whole made of two necessary beings has no reality beyond the two beings themselves. It has no third status of possibility, impossibility, or necessity beyond the necessity of each part. The same is true of a supposed whole made of two impossible things: there is no new impossibility beyond the impossibility of each part. A supposed whole made of one necessary thing and one impossible thing has only the necessity of the first and the impossibility of the second. There is nothing more.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00661

The same is true if we imagine two animals as a single whole. Each animal has its own nature. Putting them together does not create a third animal with a third nature. If one animal can speak and the other brays, the two taken together do not speak or bray as a single whole. Nor do they exist as one thing. What exists is each of the two, with no third animal made from them. We will see, in the discussion of unity, that unity cannot be separated from existence: what has no unity has no existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00662

Someone might object that if a whole made of two things that are impossible in themselves were possible in itself, then its nonexistence would be due to the lack of a cause that could bring it into existence. But the cause of the whole is the cause of its parts, and no such cause can bring these parts into existence, since they are impossible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00663

The answer is that the whole does not exist because its parts do not exist. The existence of the parts is what gives the whole existence; if the parts existed without a cause, the whole would exist as well. A cause is needed for the parts only when they are themselves possible things. When a part is impossible in itself, the whole’s nonexistence ultimately comes from that part’s necessary nonexistence. It does not lead to the absence of some other thing. The chain of existences, by contrast, ends at the Necessary Being, whose existence is necessary in itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00664
X. How a possible thing can entail something impossible in itself
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00665

Many people who discuss these questions without thinking deeply reject any necessary connection between something possible and something impossible. They assume that if something possible entails an impossibility in reality, then that possible thing must itself be impossible. Their reasoning is this: if a starting claim were possible but what follows from it were impossible, the starting claim could still hold while its necessary consequence did not. That would contradict the claim that one entails the other.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00666

If this were right, it would also rule out a link between something necessary and something possible, and even between every complete cause and its effect. A cause may be necessary when its effect is not necessary, whether the cause is necessary in itself or necessary through something else. We will explain this further.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00667

A stranger explanation appears in one set of notes: “The first claim is possible when considered in itself. What follows from it is possible in relation to that first claim, not necessarily possible when considered in itself.” When one claim entails another, what follows cannot have its opposite as something necessary in relation to the first claim. That tells us nothing about whether its opposite is necessary when considered by itself. The consequent may, in itself, be necessarily existent, necessarily nonexistent, or neither, when considered just as it is. So do not mistake this for “possibility through another,” which we have already shown to be impossible. This is possibility in relation to another, and the difference between them has been made clear.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00668

This may sound like careful reasoning, but it fails. Possibility in relation to another applies only where neither thing makes the other necessary, gives it existence, or receives existence from it. In short, there must be no necessary cause-and-effect link between them, whether in existence or nonexistence. A similarly weak explanation comes from the distinguished philosopher al-Ṭūsī. He says that the First Effect’s nonexistence would entail the nonexistence of the Necessary Being only in the sense that the First Cause would not be acting as its cause. It would not entail that the First Cause itself did not exist. The First Cause is necessary in itself, whether it has an effect or not. So, he says, the possible thing entails an impossibility only incidentally: it would be impossible for the cause, considered as a cause, not to be necessary in itself. But this is impossible only because the cause is necessary in itself, not because it is considered as a cause. This differs from the opposite case, where we suppose the First Cause itself does not exist; that would entail that the First Effect does not exist, because it receives its existence from the First Cause alone.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00669

How did so great a thinker, with such strong judgment and careful insight into divine matters, overlook that what is necessary in itself is necessary in all its descriptions? The First Cause acts as a cause because of its own essence, without waiting for some new state or additional motive. It is the self-sustaining and wholly generous source. As its essence exists, its causal power exists too; there is no real or mental separation between them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00670

Suppose the First Cause’s being a cause were merely possible, rather than necessary to its very nature. We would then have to explain the link between the First Cause and its being a cause. That link would need a further explanation, and so on without end—or we would be back at the difficulty we started with.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00671

Here is the answer. What the First Effect is can be considered possible in itself; the fact that it exists comes from the Necessary Being. Its reality therefore has two aspects, comparable to matter and form. One is need, the capacity to exist, what is hidden, and what is possible. The other is self-sufficiency, actual existence, what is revealed, and what is necessary. Our way of understanding things shows that the relations of dependence and causation among existing things arise only from their kinds of existence. An essence has no essential tie to its cause except through the existence attributed to it. We have also seen that possibility as applied to a possible existence does not mean the same thing as possibility as applied to an essence. The first goes together with necessity; the second is opposed to it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00672

Consider the First Effect in two ways. First, consider what it is. It has its own distinct identity, marked by a lack of the highest perfection and by a measure of darkness and nonexistence, although the First Reality’s light overwhelms and conceals these limits. From this point of view, its nonexistence is possible. From that side, its state of nonexistence is no different from its state of existence, from all eternity. Its essence, considered just as it is, has no share in either. Its nonexistence, considered in this way, does not entail the nonexistence of the Necessary Being, because there is no link between them on this side.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00673

Now consider it as something that exists through the First Truth. From this point of view, it cannot fail to exist, because the One who sustains its existence cannot fail to exist. Its existence entails the existence of its source, just as the existence of an effect entails the existence of the cause that brings it about. So a possible thing has not entailed something impossible. Its nonexistence in itself—that is, nonexistence considered simply as nonexistence—has no aspect of possibility, as existence has an aspect of existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00674

This does not mean that every existence is necessary in itself. We have already distinguished timeless necessity from the kind called necessity “in itself.” For the same reason, it does not mean that every nonexistence is impossible in itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00675

Someone might say: “If by the first way of considering the argument you mean that, when the mind looks only at the First Effect’s essence and considers nothing else, it finds no necessary link between it and its source, that does not prevent its nonexistence from entailing the source’s nonexistence in reality. The link remains there. But if you mean that, on this way of considering it, its nonexistence does not entail the source’s nonexistence in reality, that is plainly false. The First Effect is caused by the source in reality. How, then, could it fail to entail its cause?”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00676
I choose the second meaning. The effect is not the essence of the possible thing. Its existence is caused by the existence of its cause, and its nonexistence by the cause’s absence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00677

The same person adds: “If by the second way you mean that nonexistence which is impossible through another is not possible in itself, that is clearly wrong. Being impossible through another does not conflict with being possible in itself; it does not cancel it. The thing described by impossibility through another or necessity through another must be possible in itself, meaning that existence and nonexistence are equally open to it when considered by its own nature.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00678

I mean that nonexistence, considered simply as nonexistence, has only the aspect of impossibility, just as existence, considered simply as existence, has only the aspect of necessity. Nonexistence cannot be described as possibility of existence, any more than existence can accept nonexistence; otherwise a thing’s nature would turn into its opposite. We do not accept that the thing described by necessity through another or impossibility through another must be possible in itself in the sense that existence and nonexistence are equally open to it by its own nature. We accept this only for things other than existence and nonexistence themselves. What is necessary through another is existence linked to another; what is impossible through another is the corresponding nonexistence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00679

Here is an objection. If something possible can lead to an impossibility, as we have said, how can a proof by contradiction show that the starting assumption is impossible? For example, we argue that distance cannot be unlimited because an unlimited distance cannot be enclosed within two boundaries. Perhaps an unlimited distance is possible in itself even if its existence would entail something impossible: being enclosed between boundaries.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00680

We have already met this question and answered it. In that kind of proof, “possible” means possible in the world itself: things as they really are must allow it either to happen or not happen. Neither outcome is necessary. But the possible thing we are discussing here is an essence considered in itself, not a thing’s status in actual reality. The First Effect and other beings created directly by God are, in reality, fully actual—not merely possible. Their shadow of possibility is hidden beneath the brightness of God, the Sustainer.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00681

A thing possible in itself entails something impossible, not because of its essence but because of its nonexistence. In the same way, it entails something necessary, not because of its essence but because of its existence. The possibility used in a proof by contradiction is possibility in actual reality, not possibility at the level of an essence considered by itself. The two meanings differ. The same is true of “impossible in itself”: it may mean that nonexistence is necessary when we consider only a supposed essence, as with a partner to God or the joining of contradictories. Or it may mean that nonexistence is necessary in reality because something else requires it, whether that requirement comes from the essence or from a cause that makes it impossible in the way things exist.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00682

This is why proofs by contradiction work. If assuming that something exists leads to an impossibility, then that thing cannot exist in reality. Many arguments of the form “if this, then that” rely on the same principle. The thing may be impossible in itself because of its supposed essence, as with a partner to God or the joining of contradictories. Or something else may require it to be impossible in actual reality, because a cause fully brings about its impossibility. The conclusion is the same.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00683

For example, simple intellectual beings cannot have failed to exist in the past or cease to exist in the future. If they could cease to exist, their nonexistence would require the absence of the cause that gives them existence, and they would need matter able to receive either existence or nonexistence. Both results are impossible in themselves, as has been shown. Therefore the original assumption—that these beings could cease to exist—is impossible in actual reality too. The possibility meant in this argument is not possibility at the level of essence alone. If it were, these beings would have to be necessary in themselves, exalted far above that. You may have heard a weak argument dressed up as scholarship: anything possible must either exist or not exist, and in either state it cannot take on the opposite state. If the opposite cannot apply, then one side must be necessary, so there is no possible thing at all.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00684

Another argument says: a possible thing either exists with its complete cause present, in which case it is necessary, or exists without its complete cause, in which case it is impossible. Where, then, is there room for anything possible?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00685

People answer the first argument by saying that its division leaves out a possible case—if “exists” and “does not exist” mean that we consider the thing as either one or the other. There is a third option: we can consider its essence without either existence or nonexistence. The thing described as possible is an essence considered apart from both. Its inability to accept nonexistence in one respect, because existence has been attributed to it, does not mean that it cannot accept nonexistence in another respect; and the same applies in reverse. What makes it able to accept either side is the essence considered without those limits.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00686

If the two alternatives simply refer to a particular time, either may be chosen. But it does not follow that a thing can never take on the opposite state. All we must deny is that it can have both opposite states at once. But this is not part of the meaning of “possible,” so no problem follows. The conclusion is harmless, and the problem does not follow.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00687

The second argument’s division is also unclear if it means considering the essence and its different levels: it is either with its complete cause or without it. The second case must mean that the thing lacks the complete cause, rather than that it has the lack of the cause alongside it. If the division is about existence in reality, then it is valid. But the essence is not described as possible while it exists in reality, whether the cause is present or not. Possibility describes it in thought, when we consider it as it is in itself. So it is not true that a possible essence must either have its complete cause or lack it in reality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00688

It follows that every possible thing is surrounded either by two necessities, one earlier because its cause makes it necessary and one later because of its state in reality, or by two impossibilities on the opposite side. Neither set conflicts with what belongs to the essence when considered just as it is. That is their answer.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00689

Those who give this answer have, in effect, admitted that what a thing is does not by itself connect it to the cause that makes it exist. Before and after are features of its existence, not of what it is when considered apart from existence. An essence, considered without existence and nonexistence, cannot be clothed in either state, whether through its own nature or through a cause. It has never left, and will never leave, its hidden state into the light of appearance. In itself it remains empty, concealed, and unseen.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00690

Since an essence does not even have existence in itself, it is even less able to have the other real qualities that come after existence. None of the qualities of perfection or existence belongs to the essence except through existence. In all such qualities, the essence follows existence. Every kind of existence carries a particular essence with it. Some call this its determination; others call it its particular existence. Think of a reflection in a mirror. It follows what is in front of the mirror: its size, shape, color, movement, even its stillness. Yet all these features belong to the reflection only as an image. The reflection is not the original thing. The essence stands to existence and its qualities in the same way. Essence is an image of existence, reflected in the mind and the senses. This is why the most deeply knowing mystics and the perfected saints say that the whole world is an image within an image.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00691
Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī, a thinker devoted to knowledge of God, writes in chapter 63 of The Meccan Revelations:
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00692

“When a person sees their image in a mirror, they know for certain that they have seen their image in one sense, and have not seen it in another. The image may look very small because the mirror is small, or very large because it is large. A person cannot deny that they have seen their image, yet they know that their image is not inside the mirror, nor between the person and the mirror. They are neither truthful nor untruthful when they say, ‘I saw my image’ and ‘I did not see my image.’ What, then, is this image they see? Where is it? What is its nature? It is at once denied and affirmed, present and absent, known and unknown. God has shown His servant this truth by way of an example, so that the servant may know: if they are bewildered and unable to grasp the nature of this image, though they themselves belong to the world, then how much more unable, ignorant, and bewildered must they be before its Creator?”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00693
XI. Refuting the idea that an essence naturally favors existence or nonexistence
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00694

If you have followed what we said about what things are, and why the mind calls them possible, you will need no further argument against the claim that something, by its very nature, favors existence over nonexistence—or the reverse. This claim can mean either that a possible thing’s own nature makes one side more likely than the other, without making it necessary; or that, when the thing is considered in itself, one side fits it better than the other, though not because an outside cause makes it so.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00695

Nor can the claim mean that a thing’s own nature causes this preference in the way that something necessary in itself causes its own necessity. We have already seen that an essence has no tie to the giver of existence except through existence. Existence is given to a thing, and existence itself gives rise to effects, in different ways according to its levels of completeness, weakness, and strength. The essence, considered just as it is, has no tie to anything else. Until existence is given to it, it is nothing—not even something we can truly say is itself. We can speak of it only by imagining what it would be. Possibility may be an idea the mind draws from an essence before it exists; but until the essence enters reality and receives existence from its giver, we cannot judge that it is anything in itself or that it is possible, even if those are features that, in thought, come before its existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00696

You have learned that the mind considers an essence before considering its existence, as we consider a subject before one of its features. The same applies to what belongs to an essence in itself and what belongs to it once it exists. But outside the mind there is no subject and feature standing apart from one another. There is only existence and something that exists. The mind analyzes them and judges that some existent things involve a meaning beyond the idea of existence and being existent. It then treats one as a subject and the other as its feature—though in the world their order is the reverse. In thought, the essence comes before existence because we can grasp the essence fully, while existence cannot be grasped in its full reality. In the world, existence comes first, because existence is what is real there. The essence is joined to it only in a dependent way. This is a subtle point about why essence is an incidental feature of existence, one that most people have missed.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00697

In short, the mind calls a thing possible only when it considers what the thing is apart from its existence, setting aside the light of existence that gives it reality. Outside this mental supposition, the thing is necessary because its complete cause gives it existence. It is necessary only in that dependent sense. Considered in itself, it has no feature at all—not necessity, possibility, or anything else.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00698

The difference between a possible thing that does not exist and an impossible thing that does not exist is this: after examining it, the mind judges that the possible essence, if it were made into a real, self-standing essence, would have possibility as one of its features. The supposed impossible essence, even if we imagined it as a real, self-standing essence, would remain impossible by its own nature and could not be anything else. This does not mean that a nonexistent thing, simply as nonexistent, has possibility or impossibility. How could it, when what does not exist is no thing at all? Before something has been given existence, then, there is no independently real nature that could favor existence or anything else. To suggest that a thing makes itself and establishes its own reality, though it has no reality in itself, is not a thought a healthy mind could take seriously.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00699

Once these points are clear, we can see why a thing’s own nature cannot simply favor existence without making it necessary. The Second Teacher, Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī, points to this in a short work called The Gems of Wisdom: “If a chain of existences came about without necessity, then either a thing would bring itself into being—which is a grave mistake—or its own nonexistence would be possible, which is even worse.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00700

Here is why. If a thing exists because its own nature favors existence, it must be causing itself. If not, it has come into existence without anything making it exist, whether from within or from outside. It would therefore remain possible in itself: one side would be more likely, but not necessary. Its nonexistence would then also be possible, since it would not have been made necessary. In that case, the thing itself would be able to cease to exist, with no cause bringing about its nonexistence. This is worse than the first problem.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00701

There is a further explanation of why this is worse. A possible thing’s existence is not identical with its essence. Existence is a feature that needs an explanation. If the thing’s essence makes existence more likely, then that essence causes the thing to be described as existing, since a cause is whatever makes its effect more likely to occur. But because the essence has not made existence necessary, the thing could still fail to exist. Its nonexistence could then occur without any cause—even while the cause of its existence remains. That is sheer absurdity.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00702

This argument is needed before we have proved a Creator or established anything about reality in general. So no one can answer: “Perhaps some essences, in their existence as ideas in God’s knowledge or as forms in higher minds, incline toward existing in the outside world.” Mental existence faces the same problem as existence in the world: an essence does not exist as an essence until a giver of existence brings it into being.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00703

Even if we set aside the impossibility of this supposed inborn preference, if it were enough to make an essence exist, one and the same thing would give existence to itself and receive existence from itself. It would therefore have to exist before it exists. Beware of relying, after God has let the light of truth reach your heart from the spiritual realm, on a flash of limited reasoning that may appear along the way. One such argument comes from al-Rāzī’s commentary on The Sources of Wisdom, and others have praised it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00704

Here is that argument. If one outcome is more likely, then its opposite must be less likely, because the two descriptions go together. The less likely side must then be impossible, since it cannot prevail over the more likely side. And if the less likely side is impossible, the more likely side must be necessary. Thus, what was assumed to fall short of necessity turns out to be necessary after all, which is a contradiction.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00705

Here is the mistake. If one outcome is only more likely, the other is only less likely. Being less likely does not make it impossible. That would follow only if it were necessarily excluded, not merely less likely. In this case the less likely side is not ruled out. It is only less likely than the other side. In short, the less likely side has the same status as the side it is compared with; the more-likely side has no greater force than the side it makes less likely. If the existence side is more likely, then nonexistence is less likely, but only by way of a non-necessary preference. And if nonexistence is less likely, that too makes existence more likely, but still without making either side necessary. The two sides remain possible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00706

Even if we grant that the less-likely side is impossible when we consider the essence together with that description, the impossibility belongs to the essence only as qualified by the less-likely feature. It is therefore impossibility through another, not impossibility in itself. The preference of the other side would then be necessity through another, not necessity in itself. This does not overturn our argument. The impossibility that belongs to a description that can be removed can itself be removed; the same is true of the necessity that corresponds to it. This also undermines the other foundations people have offered on this question. Few of those arguments escape the same objection.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00707
1. Some false assumptions
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00708

Some people say that certain possible things are naturally more inclined toward existence than nonexistence, while still needing an outside cause and remaining possible. They mean that a complete cause makes these things exist more often, more fully, or with fewer conditions. Others say the reverse: that some possible things are more inclined toward nonexistence than existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00709

Some people thought that nonexistence was more likely for certain possible things. Others thought it was more likely for everything, because nonexistence is easier to bring about. Those who held these views belonged to philosophical schools from an earlier age, before philosophy had been corrected and brought to maturity. Some theologians, by contrast, say that whichever of the two sides actually occurs must have been more likely, because they deny that anything other than God can be necessary—not even something made necessary by another. A further objection follows from this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00710

Take things that never stay the same, such as sounds, time, and motion. Someone may argue that nonexistence must be more natural to them; otherwise they could last unchanged. Yet existence must also be possible for them; otherwise they would never have existed at all. If one side can be more likely than the other, why should existence not sometimes be the more likely side?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00711

Another objection starts with a cause that is present but cannot yet produce its effect. Perhaps a condition is missing, a motive has yet to arise, or an obstacle remains. Even so, the objector says, the cause must tend toward producing that effect; otherwise, why call it its cause? So before it acts, the cause must be able either to bring about its effect or not to do so, even though producing the effect is more likely. Let the same be true of the existence of an essence: it could exist more often than not, without existing every time. A cause’s effects can occur more often than not, as when the nature of earth tends to make it fall, even though a force may throw it upward and prevent the fall. Both of these claims are made up.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00712

The first claim confuses the strength or weakness of existence with the idea that existence is more likely for an essence than nonexistence. As we have explained, every thing has its own level of existence. Some have a stronger share of it; others have a weaker share, as with movement and things like it. This does not mean that existence is more likely for them than nonexistence, or the reverse. A movement’s parts do not remain fixed and continue to exist in the way that the parts of a stable thing do. They cannot. Our discussion, however, concerns existence in general and nonexistence in general, as they relate to an essence. That is what matters when we ask whether a thing is possible in itself. One particular way of existing may be impossible for it. But the thing can still, by its own nature, either exist or not exist at all.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00713

Movement and similar things that do not remain fixed are equally open to continued existence and to its absence when considered in themselves. Neither side is called for by their essence. A complete cause determines whether they exist or do not exist. If we consider them as made up of parts that all exist together, however, that kind of existence is absolutely impossible for them. We have already explained that the impossibility of one particular way of existing does not remove essential possibility in general.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00714

The second claim mistakes something that is not yet a complete cause for a cause. Before all the conditions for its effect are met, a thing is not yet acting as a cause at all. Once those conditions are met, it brings about its effect without fail. An effect may be closer to happening when fewer conditions remain to be met. But this does not make the thing itself any more or less able to exist. What changes is its readiness for the effect, which can grow stronger or weaker and is a real feature of the world. Whether a thing, considered in itself, can exist or fail to exist is a different question—one the mind answers without measuring that readiness. A thoughtful reader can use the principles already given to dismiss the wild claims made by some disputants on this subject. There is no point in listing and answering them; doing so would waste time without purpose and spend the precious days of life for no return.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00715
XII. What makes a thing need a cause: possibility in its essence and limitation in its existence
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00716

Some people make a show of reasoning and sound judgment without having learned enough to judge well. They have gone to extremes in denying the truth, and they disagree even among themselves. Some say that being brought into existence after not existing is, by itself, what makes a thing need a cause. Some say it is one part of what makes a thing need a cause. Others say it is a condition for needing a cause, while possibility itself is what makes a thing need one. Still others prepare for debate by questioning a judgment that comes naturally to the mind—a judgment present in children and even built into animals, as when an animal recoils at the sound of sticks or clubs. Their claims are not worth the time spent mocking them or the effort of wearing down one’s mind. Yet ordinary people and most students are drawn to them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00717

We say: if a feature must belong to a thing, or cannot belong to it, by the thing’s own nature, then the thing does not need something else in order to have that feature. Nor can that feature depend on something else. So if coming into existence after not existing is part of what makes a thing need a cause, whether as a condition or as one of its parts, that feature can only apply to something possible in itself—not to something necessary or impossible. In the end, then, the explanation comes back to possibility alone. That defeats the claim that origination is what makes a thing need a cause.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00718

There is another way to see this. Origination is a feature of the relation in which existence comes after nonexistence. But that relation comes after existence; existence comes after the act of bringing something into being; that act comes after the thing’s need for a cause; and that need comes after its possibility. If beginning to exist were the reason a thing needed a cause, that beginning would have to come before itself, by several steps. That is impossible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00719

Someone might object that possibility, too, is a feature of a relation to existence, and so should come later. But possibility is a state the mind assigns to the relation between the idea of existence and an essence, when it considers the essence in itself. It is not a relation that takes place in the world. So possibility follows the ideas of essence and existence as the mind considers them; it does not follow an actual relation in the world. Origination, by contrast, is a feature of something as it actually exists in the world. An essence or existence is described as originated only when it exists. Origination plainly comes after the act that gives existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00720

Those who deny the self-evidence of this claim say: “Put this judgment before the mind: existence and nonexistence are equally open to an essence in itself, so one side cannot be preferred without some cause outside it. Then put beside it the judgment that one is half of two. The second is clearer and stronger than the first. But this difference only makes sense if the first allows some doubt that the second does not. Once the opposite of a claim is possible, complete certainty is gone.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00721

Here is their mistake. Two truths can be equally certain even when one is easier to grasp than the other. How quickly someone sees a truth also varies. It depends on the ideas being considered, the person doing the thinking, and the experience they have gained. Some abilities are natural; others grow through practice. The mind learns to recognise how truths fit together much as the ear learns to hear the rhythm of words and the pattern of sounds. Both can recognise what belongs together and what does not. Anyone whose judgment is not weak or distorted, and whose mind has not been clouded by constant debate and argument, will see that one of two things alike in every respect cannot be preferred without some distinguishing cause.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00722

Whoever accepts that one thing can be preferred over an equal thing without a reason is in danger of leaving human nature behind. This comes from an evil disposition, rooted in a flawed natural capacity and an inborn rebelliousness. In the unjust village of matter and the corrupt city of the lower world, that person’s corrupted nature has taken on the darkness of false imagination.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00723

Those who accept preference without a reason have split into several groups. One group says that God created the world at one particular time rather than any other, without anything that made that time the one to choose. Another says that God assigned certain actions particular rulings—required or forbidden, good or bad—without anything in the nature of those actions calling for those rulings. Consider also someone fleeing a wild animal who reaches two roads identical in every respect, or a hungry person choosing between two identical loaves. The claim is that either person could choose one option for no reason at all.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00724

Another group says that when one of two matching things has a feature or state that the other lacks, nothing explains the difference. For if the difference had a cause, they say, the cause itself would have to be explained, and the same question would arise again. Yet another group says that all essences are equal in being essences, even though some have one feature rather than another.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00725

These are the arguments they cling to. If they woke from their ignorance, they would see that God’s creation contains causes beyond our knowledge and sight. To be unaware of a cause is not to show that no cause exists. Each of the small examples they use to deny that one matching thing can be preferred over another—the two roads, the two cups of water, and the two loaves—may have hidden factors that people who trust in chance cannot see. At the very least, there may be the alignment of heavenly bodies, the arrangement of the skies, or conditions that prepare one outcome rather than another. Beyond these lie the highest causes through which God has determined and ordered events, including the forms of things that already exist in His highest knowledge, in the fullest and most fitting way.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00726

As for the claim that the philosopher Empedocles believed in luck and chance, it seems likely that he spoke in symbols, as he and other early thinkers often did when hiding divine secrets behind images and figurative language. Some scholars explain his words this way: he denied only that God, who is necessary in Himself, acts for a purpose beyond His own essence. He still accepted that what is not necessary does not come into existence. He and others called things “by chance” when they belong to an essence not because of its own nature but because of something else. In that sense, one can say that the world’s existence is by chance. This does not mean that the world brings itself into existence or that God acts at random. It means that the world does not exist by its own nature; it exists through another.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00727

Another explanation occurs to me. As we have seen, what a possible thing is, considered apart from its existence, is only a shadow or reflection of its actual being. What is created is its existence, not its nature considered on its own. Likewise, a purpose belongs to the ways in which things exist, not to those natures taken by themselves. So the essence of the world comes about without being, in itself, the direct object of an end or an act of creation; its existence truly needs both an end and an agent. Empedocles may have called this “by chance” to mean “in a dependent or incidental way.” It resembles the aspects that, in their account, are joined to the First Effect to explain how many things can come from it even though it is simple. On that view, only one aspect—the existence of the First Effect—comes directly from the Necessary Being. Other aspects, such as its essence, its possibility, and the necessity it receives through another, come about only in a dependent way. Otherwise, many things would flow directly from what is absolutely one, or the First Being would have parts. Both are impossible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00728

The early philosophers often spoke in puzzles and symbols. Many who came after them either misunderstood their words because they did not know their place or purpose, or twisted them out of a desire to rule over people in this fleeting world. Others believed the words simply because they trusted the speaker, then openly adopted the claim that things happen by chance. They went far astray. What we should follow is certain proof or direct insight. Truth cannot be understood from words alone, since terms and languages differ, and ideas can be combined and separated in different ways. Those who say that things happen by chance have several arguments.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00729

The first is this: if a thing exists because a cause acts on it, then the cause must act either while the effect exists or while it does not exist. The first seems to produce something that already exists. The second seems to join opposites: the effect exists and does not exist at the same time. The reply turns on a distinction. A cause may act when its effect comes into being. That does not mean the effect must already exist before the cause can act. In the first statement, we are saying when the action happens. In the second, we would be making the effect’s existence a condition of the action. There is no problem with the first case. It is simply how a cause acts together with its effect: a cause and its effect exist at the same time, or at times that count as one for this purpose, and neither exists without the other. Every cause acts when its effect comes into being. It brings about the effect as such—not on the assumption that the effect already exists, nor on the assumption that it does not exist. The cause produces the effect at the very moment it comes to exist. It brings about something that has come about through that very act, not through some other act. There is no contradiction in this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00730

Here is another way to answer. If “while the effect comes into being” means that the cause and effect exist at the same time, then we choose the first option: the cause acts while the effect exists. If it means that cause and effect are together at the same level in the order of what they are, then we say the cause acts neither while the effect exists nor while it does not exist. Neither of the two problems follows. The cause acts on the essence of the effect considered just as it is, not on the essence as either existing or nonexistent. In that respect, the essence is not naturally tied to the cause. But the essence as it exists or does not exist comes after the cause’s existence or nonexistence and accompanies it in reality. Consider this carefully.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00731

Debaters have another difficult answer: the cause acts when the effect is coming into being, a state that is neither existence nor nonexistence. Some make the argument even worse by saying that the cause and effect do not have to occur together. They use sound as an example: it exists in one moment and comes from the person making it in the moment before.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00732

The second argument is that a cause must act on one of three things: the essence, its existence, or its being described as existent. The first cannot be right, they say, because whatever depends on something else would cease to exist if that other thing did not exist. But an essence cannot be removed from itself. The second cannot be right either, because then existence would stop being existence whenever the cause stopped acting. Someone may object that this would not mean a human being remained human but became “not human”; rather, the human being would simply disappear. The reply is that even “the human being is not human” is a statement that needs a subject to be settled in the judgment. We cannot both take that subject as given and deny it in the same way. If the human being disappears, the subject of the statement is gone. So what disappeared is also what was there as the subject of the denial. The thing would have to be both there and not there, settled and unsettled. The same problem applies to existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00733

The third option also fails. Saying that something has a feature establishes a link in the mind. That link cannot be the first thing a cause brings into existence: we must first have the things it links. And the relation itself has an essence, so the question returns: is the cause’s effect the relation itself, the relation’s existence, or the relation of that relation to existence? The same question would apply to each new relation, and the chain would continue without end.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00734

A well-known reply is that the act of creation is directed to the human essence itself; existence and being described as existent then follow from it because they are ideas in the mind whose basis is the essence brought about by the creator. A human being is not human because an outside agent acts on it. Rather, the human essence itself comes from another. The simple essence is the effect of the cause; it is not the more complex state of the essence being joined to itself or to something else, as in the statements “a human being is human” or “a human being exists.” A human being is human by its own nature, but its essence comes from another. The difference between these two claims is clear.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00735

If we first suppose the simple human essence itself, then its being human follows necessarily from that supposition. An outside cause cannot make it human, because what is already necessary in itself cannot depend on another for that very feature, and what has already been assumed cannot be made again. But before we suppose the human essence, the cause can bring the essence itself into being. We may say, “The human essence is necessary through the cause,” and mean the earlier kind of necessity—the necessity that comes before the thing exists.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00736

We have established the difference between necessity before a thing exists and necessity after it exists. People often confuse them because a word is used in two senses, or because they mistake something that is not a cause for a cause. A human being’s being necessary through a cause does not make the human being necessary in itself. Likewise, a human being’s dependence on a cause does not mean that its being human depends on that cause. The fact that the human essence comes from another does not show that it would cease to be human if the cause were absent. Only the fact that its being human comes from another would show that.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00737

The same applies to existence itself, which, as we have said, is brought about by a cause. Some later philosophers instead say that it is the essence itself that is brought about. We will return to the insight we have gained in this field of direct knowledge and hidden truths.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00738

The famous philosophers in Aristotle’s school choose the third option: the cause makes an essence be described as existent. They explain that what the creator brings about is a simple, undivided reality, which the mind can analyze into a subject, a feature, and the subject’s being described by that feature. In the case of a human being, the creator’s effect is what the statement “a human being exists” refers to. The effect is not just the human essence by itself, nor existence by itself, but the combined state called “the essence being described as existent.” Although this relation is an idea in the mind, it fits reality. So it must depend on a cause beyond the mind’s own thought of it: the same cause that brings about the essence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00739

What we have said shows that the three-part division was not carefully made. Consider the link we express when we say that a thing exists. We can use it simply to connect the thing with existence, without making the link itself another independent thing in our thoughts. In that role it is like a mirror: we see what it connects, not the mirror itself. But if the mind turns its attention to it separately, removing it from its role as a link, it becomes an object of thought in its own right, distinct from the two things it links. It then becomes like any other essence, and we can again ask: what aspect of it depends on the creator, and through what feature does the creator act on it? Those are among the questions people have raised.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00740
XIII. How a possible thing’s nonexistence needs a cause
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00741

Here is an objection. If something does not exist because a cause made nonexistence more likely, then the cause must somehow act on nonexistence. But nonexistence is nothing at all. How could anything act on it? Also, if a possible thing does not exist because the cause of its existence is absent, that seems to require different kinds of nonexistence—some acting as causes and others as effects. Yet absences have no distinctions or order, so there can be no cause and effect among them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00742

The answer is that nonexistence here is not simply nothing. The mind first considers what a thing would be. It then asks whether it exists or does not exist. Nothing about what it is, considered on its own, settles either question—in thought or in the world. Something beyond it is needed for one outcome rather than the other. A cause does not put something inside an essence for the essence to carry or possess in reality. Rather, it brings about something called existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00743

The existence brought about by the cause has a nature of its own, without a second act producing that nature. What the thing is takes on the colour of existence and is lit by its light for as long as that existence lasts, as we have explained. Likewise, when a cause brings about an essence’s nonexistence, all that means is that it does not bring about something that joins with the essence in a certain way—as one of its features.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00744

The mind can judge whether something exists in two ways. It can start from the cause, asking whether that cause exists and what must follow from it. Or it can start from the results: if they are present, they point to the thing’s existence; if they are absent, that can point to its absence. These are reasoning from causes and reasoning from effects.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00745

So the factor that tips the balance toward nonexistence, like the factor that tips it toward existence, must have some share in existence. Sheer nonexistence, simply as nonexistence, cannot cause anything. A cause that tips the balance toward existence must itself be something real and actual, whether or not we think about it. By contrast, what tips the balance toward nonexistence is only an idea the mind considers; it has no reality outside that act of thought. That is enough for the mind to judge that it leads to the effect’s nonexistence, both in thought and in the outside world, though in different ways.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00746

When the absence of a cause leads to the absence of an effect in the outside world, this means that neither exists at all—not even as something negative or as a relation. In the mind, by contrast, considering and affirming that the cause is absent leads us to consider and affirm that the effect is absent. The thought of the effect’s absence also leads us back to the thought that its cause is absent, but it does not make us judge that the cause is absent. In short, the mind can distinguish between ideas of absence and treat one as a reason for another. What cannot be distinguished is absence as sheer absence, and that is not what is happening here.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00747

In summary, possible essences and other settled realities have states and relations that the mind considers before they exist in the outside world. The mind arranges some of these ideas in relation to others, though nothing outside the mind corresponds to them. Outside the mind, there is only existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00748

The mind then pictures an essence as joined with existence, while recognizing that the idea of essence differs from the idea of existence. Considered in itself, the essence is bare of both existence and nonexistence: neither is necessary to it, and neither is ruled out. The mind therefore concludes that for either to be realized, something beyond the essence must tip the balance. Our reasoning therefore takes this order: the thing is possible; it needs a cause; the cause makes its existence necessary; the cause brings it into being; and the thing exists.
